To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the small cysteines-rich proteins of C psittaci and C. trachomatis are lipoproteins.
the mature EnvA is a small cysteine-containing protein that is lipid modified, and it is hydrophobic, despite its predicted hydrophilic peptide sequence.

the small cysteines-rich protein of C. psitacci 6BC (EnvA) lacks its N-terminal methionin, is lipid modified at an cysteine residue, and is similar in fatty acid composition to the murein lipopeptide of E. coli and to the small cysteins-rich protein of C.trachomatis L 2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the small cystine-rich proteins of the chlamydiae and the possible role of these proteins in the pathogenesis of chlamydial infections.
the identification of a novel class of proteins, the small cysteines, and their role in the biology of the chlamydiae.
the characterization of a novel lipoprotein of chlamydiae and its role in the biology of the chlamydial cell.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the EnvA proteins of C. trachomatis and C. psittacci are murein lipopeptides.
EnvA is a lipoprotein and that the small cysteines of the other cysteine-rich lipoproteins are not lipid modified.

the small cysteines of C. psitacci and C. trachomatis are lipidated by a fatty acid of 16 carbons in length and that the lipid is attached to the cysteine by an amide bond, with the fatty acid in the sn-2 position.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the small cysteines of the small cysteinic proteins of chlamydia are modified with palmitic or palmitoleic acid in a manner similar to that of the lipoprotein signal sequence of gram-negative bacteria and the lipoprotein EnvE of Chlamydiaceae.
the small cysteines of the small cystine-rich proteins are lipid modified and that the mature proteins are hydrophobic.
the small cysteines of EnvA and the homologous protein of C. trachomatis are lipid modified and are not glycosylated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the small cysteines of EnvA and its homologues are likely to be lipid modified.
EnvA of C. psititaci is a murein lipopeptide, and that the EnvA of C.trachomatis may also be a murein-like lipopeptide.
EnvA is a small, lipid-modified, hydrophobic, cysteine-rich, and highly conserved chlamydial protein.
